Using TMB

Source: vignettes/articles/tmb.qmd

TMB (Kristensen et al., 2016) compiles a log-density written as a C++ template, and computes its gradient by automatic differentiation. The gradient is exact, and nothing has to be derived by hand. inla_vanilla() takes TMB’s objective and gradient as they are, apart from the sign: TMB minimises.

This article fits the industrialisation and political democracy model of Bollen (1989), a structural equation model with 39 parameters. The article Speeding up with Rcpp describes the model, its unconstrained parameterisation, the priors and their Jacobians, and writes the same log-posterior in R and in C++. Here we write it as a TMB template.

library(inlavanilla)
data(PoliticalDemocracy, package = "lavaan")

Data and parameters

The 11 indicators, in the order x1, x2, x3, y1, …, y8, and the six pairs with correlated residuals:

ov <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", paste0("y", 1:8))
Y <- as.matrix(PoliticalDemocracy[, ov])

cov_pairs <- rbind(
  c("y1", "y5"),
  c("y2", "y4"),
  c("y2", "y6"),
  c("y3", "y7"),
  c("y4", "y8"),
  c("y6", "y8")
)

The 39 parameters, all on an unconstrained scale, in six blocks:

Block Number Parameters Prior
nu 11 intercepts \(N(0, 32^2)\)
lam 5 loadings of x2, x3, and a, b, c \(N(0, 10^2)\)
beta 3 regressions \(N(0, 10^2)\)
logv_lv 3 log variance of ind60, log disturbance variances of dem60 and dem65 \(\text{Gamma}(1, \text{rate } 0.5)\) on the SD
logv_ov 11 log residual variances \(\text{Gamma}(1, \text{rate } 0.5)\) on the SD
z 6 residual correlations \(\rho\) on the atanh scale \(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\) on \((\rho + 1)/2\)

We give them readable names, and the same starting values as in the Rcpp article:

parnames <- c(
  paste0("nu_", ov),
  c("lam_x2", "lam_x3", "a", "b", "c"),
  c("beta_dem60_ind60", "beta_dem65_ind60", "beta_dem65_dem60"),
  paste0("logv_", c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")),
  paste0("logv_", ov),
  paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])
)
init <- c(
  colMeans(Y),
  rep(1, 5),
  rep(0, 3),
  rep(0, 3),
  log(apply(Y, 2, var) / 2),
  rep(0, 6)
)
names(init) <- parnames

The template

A TMB template declares its data and parameters, and returns the value to minimise, here the negative log-posterior. density::MVNORM_t is TMB’s multivariate normal; it returns the negative log-density, normalising constant included. The 75 pointwise log-likelihoods are kept in a vector, and REPORT() makes them available from R. The log-prior adds the log-Jacobians of the standard deviations and correlations, as in the Rcpp article.

tmb_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "sem_tmb.cpp")
#include <TMB.hpp>

template <class Type>
Type objective_function<Type>::operator()() {
  DATA_MATRIX(Y);            // 75 x 11: x1, x2, x3, y1, ..., y8

  PARAMETER_VECTOR(nu);      // 11 intercepts
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(lam);     // loadings: x2, x3, then a, b, c
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(beta);    // dem60 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ ind60, dem65 ~ dem60
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(logv_lv); // log variances of ind60, dem60, dem65
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(logv_ov); // log residual variances, x1 to y8
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(z);       // residual correlations, atanh scale

  int n = Y.rows(), p = Y.cols();

  // Loadings, with the first of each latent variable fixed at 1, and a, b, c
  // shared between 1960 and 1965
  matrix<Type> Lambda(p, 3);
  Lambda.setZero();
  Lambda(0, 0) = 1;
  Lambda(1, 0) = lam(0);
  Lambda(2, 0) = lam(1);
  Lambda(3, 1) = 1;
  Lambda(4, 1) = lam(2);
  Lambda(5, 1) = lam(3);
  Lambda(6, 1) = lam(4);
  Lambda(7, 2) = 1;
  Lambda(8, 2) = lam(2);
  Lambda(9, 2) = lam(3);
  Lambda(10, 2) = lam(4);

  matrix<Type> B(3, 3);
  B.setZero();
  B(1, 0) = beta(0);
  B(2, 0) = beta(1);
  B(2, 1) = beta(2);
  matrix<Type> I(3, 3);
  I.setIdentity();
  matrix<Type> A = atomic::matinv(matrix<Type>(I - B));

  vector<Type> psi = exp(logv_lv);
  vector<Type> v = exp(logv_ov);
  vector<Type> rho = tanh(z);
  matrix<Type> Psi = psi.matrix().asDiagonal();
  matrix<Type> Theta = v.matrix().asDiagonal();
  // Residual covariances: y1-y5, y2-y4, y2-y6, y3-y7, y4-y8, y6-y8
  int ci[6] = {3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 8};
  int cj[6] = {7, 6, 8, 9, 10, 10};
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    Theta(ci[k], cj[k]) = rho(k) * sqrt(v(ci[k]) * v(cj[k]));
    Theta(cj[k], ci[k]) = Theta(ci[k], cj[k]);
  }

  matrix<Type> LA = Lambda * A;
  matrix<Type> Sigma = LA * Psi * LA.transpose() + Theta;

  // Pointwise log-likelihood
  density::MVNORM_t<Type> mvn(Sigma);
  vector<Type> loglik(n);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    vector<Type> r = vector<Type>(Y.row(i)) - nu;
    loglik(i) = -mvn(r);
  }
  REPORT(loglik);

  // Log-prior on the unconstrained scale, with the Jacobians
  Type logprior = sum(dnorm(nu, Type(0), Type(32), true)) +
    sum(dnorm(lam, Type(0), Type(10), true)) +
    sum(dnorm(beta, Type(0), Type(10), true));
  vector<Type> logv(14);
  logv << logv_lv, logv_ov;
  for (int k = 0; k < 14; k++) {
    // Gamma(1, rate 0.5) on the SD (TMB's dgamma() takes the scale), and
    // d SD / d logv = SD / 2
    Type sd = exp(logv(k) / Type(2));
    logprior += dgamma(sd, Type(1), Type(1 / 0.5), true) + log(sd / Type(2));
  }
  for (int k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
    // Beta(1, 1) on (rho + 1) / 2, and d rho / d z = 1 - rho^2
    Type u = (rho(k) + Type(1)) / Type(2);
    logprior += dbeta(u, Type(1), Type(1), true) - log(Type(2)) +
      log(Type(1) - rho(k) * rho(k));
  }

  return -(sum(loglik) + logprior);
}

Compiling

TMB::compile() builds a shared library from the template, which takes a minute or so. TMB::MakeADFun() then records the computation and returns an object whose fn and gr evaluate the objective and its gradient. The parameters go in as a list of the six vectors, and obj$par holds them in one vector, in the same order as init.

invisible(TMB::compile(tmb_file))
dyn.load(TMB::dynlib(sub("\\.cpp$", "", tmb_file)))

blocks <- rep(
  c("nu", "lam", "beta", "logv_lv", "logv_ov", "z"),
  c(11, 5, 3, 3, 11, 6)
)
obj <- TMB::MakeADFun(
  data = list(Y = Y),
  parameters = split(unname(init), factor(blocks, unique(blocks))),
  DLL = "sem_tmb",
  silent = TRUE
)
all.equal(unname(obj$par), unname(init))
#> [1] TRUE

A check against INLAvaan

INLAvaan fits the same model, with the same parameterisation and priors. As in the Rcpp article, we put its posterior mode in our order:

model <- "
  ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3
  dem60 =~ y1 + a*y2 + b*y3 + c*y4
  dem65 =~ y5 + a*y6 + b*y7 + c*y8
  dem60 ~ ind60
  dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60
  y1 ~~ y5
  y2 ~~ y4 + y6
  y3 ~~ y7
  y4 ~~ y8
  y6 ~~ y8
"
fit_inlavaan <- INLAvaan::asem(
  model,
  PoliticalDemocracy,
  meanstructure = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
int <- INLAvaan::get_inlavaan_internal(fit_inlavaan)

lv <- c("ind60", "dem60", "dem65")
inlavaan_names <- c(
  paste0(ov, "~1"),
  "ind60=~x2",
  "ind60=~x3",
  "a",
  "b",
  "c",
  "dem60~ind60",
  "dem65~ind60",
  "dem65~dem60",
  paste0(c(lv, ov), "~~", c(lv, ov)),
  paste0(cov_pairs[, 1], "~~", cov_pairs[, 2])
)
at <- match(inlavaan_names, names(int$coefficients))
theta_inlavaan <- setNames(int$theta_star_novbc[at], parnames)

There, the template’s objective should equal the one INLAvaan minimised:

c(TMB = obj$fn(theta_inlavaan), INLAvaan = int$opt$objective)
#>      TMB INLAvaan 
#> 1655.078 1655.078

Fitting

TMB’s fn returns the negative log-posterior and gr its gradient as a one-row matrix, so we negate both and flatten the gradient. With init as the starting values, the parameters keep our names; obj$par would also do, and its repeated names (nu, nu, …) would be numbered.

fit <- inla_vanilla(
  function(theta) -obj$fn(theta),
  init,
  grad = function(theta) -as.vector(obj$gr(theta))
)
#> ✔ Found the posterior mode in 91 iterations [54ms]
#> ✔ VB mean correction, max shift 0.43σ [1.2s]
#> ✔ Fitted 39 skew-normal marginals [705ms]

inla_vanilla() checks the gradient against finite differences at init, and would warn if it disagreed. The calls, and the time per call in microseconds:

time_per_call <- function(f, n) {
  elapsed <- system.time(
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      f()
    }
  )[["elapsed"]]
  1e6 * elapsed / n
}
fit$counts
#> logpost    grad 
#>    1537    9933
c(
  fn = time_per_call(function() obj$fn(init), n = 2000),
  gr = time_per_call(function() obj$gr(init), n = 1000)
)
#>    fn    gr 
#>  58.5 146.0

A gradient costs a few evaluations of the objective, against 40 for finite differences. Without it, the fit would take over 20,000 evaluations of the objective. A hand-written gradient, as in the Rcpp article, can be faster still, but it has to be derived and checked; TMB’s needs neither.

This agrees with the Rcpp article’s fit, which uses the same log-posterior, to within about \(10^{-4}\) posterior SDs. The two checks flagged by summary() are the ridge bend and the gap between the skew-normal and VB means, both for logv_dem65; the Rcpp article discusses them.

plot(fit, pars = paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2]))

On the natural scale

The parameters are on the unconstrained scale, and sampling() with fun maps its draws back. Here are the residual correlations \(\rho = \tanh z\) and the disturbance variance of dem65, next to the posterior medians from INLAvaan’s own copula draws, which are on the natural scale.

set.seed(2026)
natural <- sampling(fit, nsamp = 10000, fun = function(theta) {
  rho <- tanh(theta[paste0("z_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])])
  names(rho) <- paste0("rho_", cov_pairs[, 1], "_", cov_pairs[, 2])
  c(rho, psi_dem65 = exp(theta[["logv_dem65"]]))
})
draws <- INLAvaan::sampling(fit_inlavaan, nsamp = 10000)
v <- function(x) draws[, paste0(x, "~~", x)]
rho <- draws[, paste0(cov_pairs[, 1], "~~", cov_pairs[, 2])] /
  sqrt(v(cov_pairs[, 1]) * v(cov_pairs[, 2]))
round(
  cbind(
    t(apply(natural, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))),
    INLAvaan = c(apply(rho, 2, median), median(v("dem65")))
  ),
  3
)
#>             2.5%   50% 97.5% INLAvaan
#> rho_y1_y5 -0.024 0.288 0.528    0.286
#> rho_y2_y4  0.039 0.276 0.475    0.274
#> rho_y2_y6  0.153 0.345 0.520    0.345
#> rho_y3_y7 -0.084 0.184 0.421    0.184
#> rho_y4_y8 -0.158 0.109 0.347    0.111
#> rho_y6_y8  0.080 0.315 0.509    0.317
#> psi_dem65  0.028 0.234 0.739    0.230

The medians agree with INLAvaan’s, up to the Monte Carlo error of the two sets of draws. The disturbance variance of dem65 is small and poorly determined, with a long right tail on this scale.

Leave-one-out cross-validation

obj$report() evaluates the template at any parameter value without recording derivatives, and returns the 75 pointwise log-likelihoods: the loglik that loo() needs. It leaves out one country at a time, from this one fit:

loo_sem <- loo(fit, function(theta) obj$report(theta)$loglik)
loo_sem
#> ── Leave-one-out cross-validation ────────────────────────────── 75 units ──
#> 
#>           Estimate    SE
#> elpd_loo   -1588.8  20.5
#> p_loo         38.6   3.0
#> looic       3177.7  40.9
#> 
#> ✔ Second-order expansion for every unit. Largest leverage k = 0.25, for
#>   unit 35.

INLAvaan’s loo() uses the same deterministic expansion (Alhyari et al., 2026), with its own per-case log-likelihoods:

loo_inlavaan <- INLAvaan::loo(fit_inlavaan)
round(
  rbind(
    ours = loo_sem$estimates[, "Estimate"],
    INLAvaan = loo_inlavaan$estimates[, "Estimate"]
  ),
  2
)
#>          elpd_loo p_loo   looic
#> ours     -1588.83 38.61 3177.67
#> INLAvaan -1588.96 38.77 3177.92

The two agree to well within the standard error. They differ a little because each expands about its own VB-corrected mean, and the two VB corrections take their expectations with different rules.

With 39 parameters this takes \(39^2 + 39 + 1\), or 1,561, evaluations of the template, each giving all 75 terms. See Model comparison with LOO and WAIC for what the numbers mean and how to compare models with them.

References

Alhyari, M., Jamil, H., Montcho, H., & Rue, H. (2026). Deterministic leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation for multilevel Bayesian models (arXiv:2609.00670 [stat.ME]). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.00670

Bollen, K. A. (1989). Structural equations with latent variables. Wiley. https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118619179

Kristensen, K., Nielsen, A., Berg, C. W., Skaug, H., & Bell, B. M. (2016). TMB: Automatic differentiation and Laplace approximation. Journal of Statistical Software, 70(5), 1–21. https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v070.i05
